analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis of nMPRA Processor based on Multithreaded Execution

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This article presents several solutions meant to improve the performance of CPU architecture and it describes a fine-grained multithreading architecture empowered with a hardware scheduler that uses remapping techniques for the program counter, the register file and the pipeline registers. In this context, our main contribution relates to a custom CPU implementation in order to provide predictability execution for hard real-time tasks. Experimental data obtained during tests is analyzed in order to validate the proposed CPU, based on a finegrained multithreading architecture and a fast switching operation between a blocked task and another one, scheduled by Hardware Scheduler Engine (nHSE). The resource differences between the original Multi Pipeline Register Architecture (nMPRA) implementation and the multithreading configuration are also taken in consideration.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time embedded systems are those systems that provide a correct answer within a predetermined time interval [1]. Nevertheless, in critical applications, it proves insufficient to receive a correct answer after the deadline, and it can no longer be taken into consideration [2].

Guaranteeing determinism is very important in hard realtime systems. Apart from the fact that a cache memory ensures more performance and decreases access time to the data or code, this technology can be used successfully in providing constant access time to task code instructions. During the period of operation of a real-time system (RTS), program instructions may be rewritten by a new task. When resuming the execution of the old interrupted task, these instructions will have to be brought back from the code memory, thus causing an additional override.

Embedded and FPGA systems have developed significantly over the last few years. As a result, we can obtain, at lower prices, a high number of gates that allow the implementation of a processor in hardware. FPGA devices, at efficient costs and a high capacity of logical gates [3], can represent a hardware support for embedded operating systems.

By moving the operating systems or some of its components into the hardware, we intend to exclude the variable execution time of the real-time operating system (RTOS) and most of the sources of non-determinism that have been introduced by external asynchronous interrupts.

The motivation of this paper is represented by the inconvenience identified in actual RTOSs that run on microcontrollers, which refers to the variable execution time primarily results from the number of tasks, the type of scheduler, and the data dependency introduced by the pipeline assembly line.

Two trends in RTOS-based hardware design have been developed in the last few years: a minor one, based on the specialized processors, and a major one, which involves coprocessors or scheduling accelerators. Real-time operating systems can be divided into software RTOS, mixed RTOS (where the scheduler is implemented through the hardware), and hardware RTOS.

Using an FPGA device, we intend to obtain an original implementation with thread interleaved pipelines, static or dynamic scheduling of the tasks, and interrupts with hardwarebased isolation. The main reasons for the implementation of nMPRA processor into the hardware are the following:
• reducing the memory footprint.
• jitter reduction.
• reducing the override generated by basic RTOS functions, such as task scheduling, task switching, and operating system overhead.

This paper is structured as follows: after a brief introduction in the first section, the related work is presented in section II. Subsequently, section III and IV gives an overview of the nMPRA and nMPRA-MT architectures. The impact of different CPU configuration models on FPGA resources and the experimental results achieved during tests, are presented in section V, while section VI concludes the paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Many researchers have proposed and validated various processor architectures, each of them making compromises to meet the requirements of the application. Further on, we intend to present and analyze some new architectures, partially or totally implemented through the hardware.

Rochange and Sainrat in [4] have suggested modifications in the pipelines of the dynamic superscalar processors by slowing down the instructions between blocks. The authors addressed the idea of out-of-order speculative execution using a six-stage pipeline. This architecture was designed so that the time spent by the base blocks would be independent from one block to another. This is caused by the slowing down process of instruction fetching from a base block until the instructions from the prior block are executed.

PRET (Precision Timed Machine) architecture is mainly based on two important features. The first refers to the system ability to integrate new valid components, in full compliance with the system timing behavior. Therefore, if during integration, the characteristics of the components are destroyed, the components can no longer be designed and checked separately [5]. The second feature of PRET architecture is predictability and it involves the ability to ensure and improve the average case execution time (ACET). Conventional architectures introduced cache memories, prediction and speculation units, in order to improve the worst case execution time (WCET) [6], [7]. To accomplish this, PRET architecture uses partitioned scratchpad memories for all PRET tasks [8], the scheduling pattern being implemented into the software. Since memory allocation takes place in the software, its content is known due to an exact and efficient analysis. Since each task is linked to a DRAM memory bank, the memory refresh operation can be conducted separately for each thread when operations involving it are not scheduled.

The SPEAR processor proposed by Delvai et al. [9] features a 16-bit architecture that executes instructions over a three-stage pipeline and no cache memory. This processor architecture is mainly grounded on a single-path execution and a constant instruction time. It runs on a maximum frequency of 40 MHz and comprises a set of 32 registers, of which 26 are general purpose registers, and 6 registers have special functions. Some of these functions are either the instructions dedicated to efficiently implement stacks, or the ones used to save the return address in case of subroutines calls or exceptions. The SPEAR concept based on a single-path execution and a three-stage pipeline simplifies the complex problems generated by WCET, guaranteeing at the same time system predictability.

div.head: III. OVERVIEW OF THE NMPRA ARCHITECTURE
div.p: In the nMPRA processor, each thread has an independent set of pipeline registers with a major role in reducing the time needed for task switching [10]. This project aims at to obtaining a RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computing) processor that could meet the demands of a real-time system, by using a FPGA-based development board. Hardware implementation of scheduling patterns and the significant reduction in switching time have led to a competitive and innovative architecture [10], [11].

With each task switching, the nHSE remaps the PC, the register file bank, and the pipeline registers, in order to restore the processor internal state for that task. The nHSE scheduler is responsible for the following operations:
• bank switching in the register file.
• pipeline register switching.
• synchronization with mutexes and simple semaphores.
• interrupts and timers management.
• executing static or dynamic scheduling operations.

div.head: IV. NMPRA-MT ARCHITECTURE AND HARDWARE SUPPORT
div.p: This paper aims at continuing and extending the nMPRA concept presented by Gaitan et al. in [10]. It would be very useful to put forth the nMPRA architecture described by Dodiu et al. in [11] for multithreading configuration, by extending its already existing semantics needed for embedded control in mixed-criticality systems. To achieve this, authors have chosen to replicate the general purpose registers, pipeline registers, and program counter, guaranteeing the predictable behavior of all hard real-time concurrent tasks.

The nMPRA-MT architecture (Multi Pipeline Register Architecture -Fine-Grained Multithreading) is an innovative CPU project aiming to improve the predictability of execution and of interrupt handling mechanisms [12]. The interrupts inherit the priority of the tasks to which they are attached, being scheduled by nHSE in order to meet the deadline [13]. The authors classify the hard real-time threads as Hard Threads-HT, and non real-time threads as Soft Threads-ST (we will use the terms "thread" and "task" interchangeably).

div.head: A. Pipeline and Thread Management
div.p: Task parallelization increases pipeline efficiency while performance is not reduced by the data, structural or control hazards. As can be seen in Fig. 1, the nMPRA-MT processor can no longer encounter unresolved data hazard situations due to the data used by an instruction which has not yet been produced by the previous instruction. In case of a jump instruction, the pipeline empty operation is no longer necessary. Fig. 1 depicts two generic examples with different threads which are dynamically scheduled in the pipeline assembly line. To accomplish this, each pipeline level is occupied by threads with different priorities. For an accurate use of wasted CPU cycles, the STs are inserted into the pipeline when the HTs are in the sleep or idle state.

The first example, presented in Fig. 1.a, takes place when the HT threads 0 and 1 are scheduled to be executed every two clock cycles, providing that these threads meet their deadline. As we can see, the 0 thread depicted in red is scheduled by nHSE in CC1, CC3 and CC5 clock cycles, while 1 thread depicted in blue is scheduled on CC2 and CC4. The second example describes the situation when the HT thread 1 is placed in idle state, and 0 thread continues to run until it reaches its deadline. As can be seen in Fig. 1.b, the 0 thread maintains the execution timeframe and the three ST threads 2 , 3 and 4 have been scheduled by using the roundrobin algorithm implemented by nHSE.

Therefore, the scheduler achieves full charge of the pipeline assembly line based on a very fast task switching technique. Seeing this, we can argue that the calculation of a WCET is a complicated but achievable goal, the processor becoming deterministic.

div.head: B. Events and Resource Management
div.p: With an independent execution, the nHSE has inputs for events such as interrupts or timers. As can be noticed in Fig. 2, the o i commands represent the enable signals for the threads and used by the nHSE unit. When the scheduler is enabled by the relative signal, the block diagram decodes at the same time the ID and STATE register of five active threads. At a given moment, five such o i valid commands can be present simultaneously on the output. This is possible by using the dynamic nHSE scheduler, the synchronization signals and registers and the block dedicated to the events.

div.head: V. VALIDATION OF THE NMPRA ARCHITECTURE
div.p: The nMPRA project has been developed on a FPGA from Xilinx (xc6vlx240t-1ff1156), whereas the processor coding was developed in standard Verilog, as we can see in the Fig. 3.

Various configurations of the nMPRA processor, with 4, 8 and 16 tasks, have been validated for a 10 MHz, 50 MHz and 75 MHz operation frequency. Since the system has a higher number of tasks than the number of pipeline stages, it is necessary to know which task is probable to reach its deadline. Therefore, a new task may be introduced, without penalties in the pipeline assembly line.

The dynamic scheduler has been specially designed to provide predictability of execution and spatial isolation for HTs, but it simultaneously schedules the STs to use any available cycle. Soft threads-ST represent the tasks where a missing deadline does not cause a critical effect, but are useful tools to complete the system. The scheduler controls an arbitrary number of threads interlacing with the pipeline levels. The nHSE represents a hardware scheduling interface for the nMPRA-MT RTOS and also for the local memory dedicated to HT and ST threads. The real-time scheduler is specially designed to ensure inter-task synchronization and communication, being also responsible with the scheduling algorithm for accessing the free CPU cycles.

div.head: A. Experimental Results
div.p: When the CPU is powered or reset, the local nHSE will start running at 'EXC_V_Base0_Reset'. All the other exceptions are made up of the base address and the offset. The base address is either a bootstrap or normal value, controlled by one bit in the 'Status_reg' register. Both base addresses can be mapped to the same location. The offset address is either a standard offset, or a special interrupt-only offset for interrupts, which is enabled with one bit in the first HT thread 'Cause_reg' register. At a 50 MHz frequency, the scheduler answer to an asynchronous external event may be around 26 ns. The internal logic of the nHSE block needs at least 6 ns to perform task scheduling and remapping sequence of the contexts. For the case in which the program executes sw instructions, at an operating frequency of 50 MHz, the scheduler answer to an asynchronous external event can be up to 67 ns.

A basic mixed-criticality example with two hard real-time tasks, 0 and 2 was simulated on the nMPRA-MT architecture, as a more concrete validation test of the interferences between HTs and STs. In order to accomplish a fast context switch, each task has a PC, a distinct bank in the register file and an independent set of pipeline registers (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, and MEM/WB). Therefore, as we can see in Fig. 4, at 10 MHz the contexts switch are performed by register set remapping; this way, either the CPU runs with the global memory or not, task switching is guaranteed in one or three clock cycles (a maximum delay of 300 ns -three machine cycles). The internal logic block of the nHSE requires no more than 40 ns to achieve the scheduling and remapping sequence of the contexts. At the same time, in order to monitor the application answer, we used a registered port with an internal D flip-flop to memorize the state. This D flip-flop is written on the falling edge of the nMPRA_clock, as an additional reason of delay. This means that these ports do not use additional D flip-flop to memorise the internal state: on the contrary, they generate the logical value written on the port directly on its associated exit. This type of port was used to obtain a realistic evaluation of the scheduler answer and to exclude possible delays caused by the synchronization, using the system clock to write on the port.

div.head: B. The Impact of Different Processor Configurations on FPGA Resources
div.p: The nHSE and Hazard Detection/Forward Unit represents the main source that increases the total processor area costs, shown by flip-flop (FF) and lookup-table (LUT) in Fig. 5. The increase in LUTs and FFs in the nMPRA and nMPRA-MT architecture is caused by the differences in attaching the additional logic of multithreading architecture.

The difference of resources between the original nMPRA and nMPRA-MT architecture is due to those applications that need predictability and isolated hard real-time threads. This architecture was designed especially to decrease the jitter and the over-control due to the scheduler. The nHSE is taskoriented, tasks having a constant priority within the dynamic execution at pipeline level in order to increase the throughput of execution.

The validated implementation is essential for assessing correctness and validity and for monitoring timing behavior of the proposed feasible set of tasks. The hard or soft real-time tasks have different criticality levels, being designed to satisfy the predictability for hard real-time applications.

Unlike the other projects proposed in the recent literature which are a hardware-software combination, inferentially leading to a longer task switching time interval, the nMPRA-MT concept, including the integrated nHSE scheduler, represent a hardware implementation based on the idea that it does neither affect the pipeline, nor does it require register saving when perform context switching operations. The limitations of the current CPU implementations are given by a non-PRET approach into the design level of the CPU, memory, I/O subsystem and high level languages and compilers. The difficulty elements of the problem are given by the obtaining architecture PRET type, at the microarchitecture level, but also in the RTOS, by incorporating its functionality in hardware and performance improvement, highlighting the predictable behavior.

div.head: C. Field of Applications
div.p: Given below are several examples of applications which can successfully use the architecture of the new processor that implements four or eight tasks, with static or dynamic scheduling.

1) The Automotive Field. a) the cylinder fuel injection system, where each injector is managed by a task. b) direction management system for four steered wheels, ABS (Antilock Braking System) and ESC (Electronic Stability Control) motor vehicles.

2) The Robotics Field. a) the implemented processor can successfully use a static scheduling pattern to manage linear and rotational measurement systems. Two tasks perform the reading and processing of those signals that correspond to a single axis, while two are used to ensure system safety functions.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: This processor architecture is scalable, slightly extensible, depending on the characteristics of the FPGA used and on the type of processor implemented. Designing coprocessors or schedulers into the hardware is a novelty to real-time systems and a real challenge in the field. This being said, we test the jitter reduction of our processor implementation which supports hardware-based isolation for HTs, allowing, at the same time, the efficient use of the CPU cycles for STs. The STs can share the unused processor cycle using standard scheduling algorithms, such as the round-robin.

Nevertheless, the approximated implementation percentage costs relative to the FPGA device used for validation (Xilinx Virtex-6 xc6vlx240t-1ff1156) may increase with a large number of threads and with a more complex functionality, like inter-task synchronization and communication mechanisms.

For the future, we will consider designing the nHSE scheduling unit with various scheduling algorithms. For soft threads we have to provide an acceptable number of clock cycles, complying thus with all system requirements.
